summary.text: A quadratic equation contains only non-negative whole-number powers of x, so it is a second-degree polynomial equation.
With real coefficients it has zero, one or two distinct real roots, and always two roots when complex ones count and a double root counts twice.
It can be solved by factoring, by completing the square or by a formula in a, b and c, and such problems were known as early as 2000 BC.

facts.label: Real roots
facts.value: Zero, one or two distinct real roots

facts.label: Double root
facts.value: One distinct root counts as two equal roots

facts.label: No real roots
facts.value: Two complex roots, conjugates of each other

facts.label: Oldest records
facts.value: Quadratic problems were solved as early as 2000 BC

items.prompt: To factor x² + 5x + 6, you look for two numbers that add to 5 and multiply to 6. Which pair?

options.label: 1 and 6
2 and 3
1 and 5
3 and 4

items.explain: The pair must add to b and multiply to c, which is why x² + 5x + 6 factors as (x + 3)(x + 2).

items.prompt: You know (x + 3)(x + 2) = 0. What must be true?

options.label: Both brackets must equal zero together
Both brackets must equal each other
At least one bracket equals zero
The brackets must add up to zero

items.explain: The Zero Factor Property says the equation holds if px + q = 0 or rx + s = 0, so one factor is zero.

items.prompt: Which count of distinct real solutions can a quadratic with real coefficients never have?

options.label: Three
Zero
One
Two

items.explain: Such an equation has zero, one or two distinct real roots.

items.prompt: Why can most quadratics in practical problems not be solved by factoring by inspection?

options.label: It needs the x term to be missing
It works only for rational roots, and most roots are not
It only works when a is bigger than 1
It always requires trial with decimals

items.explain: Factoring by inspection works only for quadratics with rational roots, which excludes the great majority in practice.

items.prompt: A quadratic with real coefficients has no real roots. What is still true?

options.label: It has two complex roots that are conjugates
It has no roots of any kind
It has one complex root
It has two real roots after rounding

items.explain: The equation still has two complex-valued roots, complex conjugates of each other.

items.prompt: A friend says a quadratic equation with complex-number coefficients could have no roots at all. Is that right?

options.label: Yes, complex coefficients can wipe out every root
Yes, but only if the two roots would be equal
No, it always has exactly one real-valued root
No, it always has two complex roots, maybe equal

items.explain: A quadratic equation with arbitrary complex coefficients always has two complex-valued roots, which may or may not be distinct.
